claims.text: Integrating an oxygen sublattice buffer during bottom-up synthesis will mitigate high-temperature cation migration in near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles.
Integrating an oxygen sublattice buffer will mitigate high-temperature phase segregation in near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles.
An oxygen sublattice buffer will preserve the structural and chemical homogeneity of HEA nanoparticles under service conditions.
Conventional bottom-up HEA nanoparticles without an engineered oxygen sublattice are prone to cation migration and phase segregation at elevated temperatures.
Controlled incorporation of oxide precursors during nanoparticle formation can produce an internal oxygen scaffold.
The relevant catalytic service-temperature range is 773–1173 K.
The relevant thermoelectric service-temperature range is 473–1923 K.
An engineered oxygen sublattice can act as a buffer layer within a compositionally complex material.
The oxygen buffer stabilizes the crystal lattice by reducing cation mobility.
Reduced cation mobility limits cation migration and phase segregation at high temperature.
The proposed stabilization maintains a near-equiatomic, single-phase structure.
Maintaining a near-equiatomic, single-phase structure is critical for catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Buffered nanoparticles will exhibit less phase segregation after high-temperature treatment than unbuffered controls.
Buffered nanoparticles will retain a more uniform elemental distribution after high-temperature treatment than unbuffered controls.
Buffered nanoparticles will retain catalytic or thermoelectric activity better than unbuffered controls after high-temperature treatment.
The magnitude of structural stabilization and performance retention may depend on nanoparticle composition and detailed synthesis parameters.
